newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Who pays, wins - but maybe not in British election.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Who pays, wins - but maybe not in British election.

text.p: Britain's Conservatives have a saying -- better to wake up the morning after election day bankrupt but in office, than solvent and in opposition.
At the last election, they took this to heart, borrowing from banks for the first time to fund their campaign.
The ruling party shelled out 11 million pounds ($17.66 million) to Labour's 10.4 million. But it was money well spent as the Conservatives claimed their fourth victory in a row.
Ahead of the May 1 election, the Conservatives have managed to turn a mid-term deficit of more than 15 million pounds into a huge "war-chest", put by newspapers at up to 40 million pounds.
But with polls pointing to a Labour victory, this election may be the last to be held under current party funding rules which opponents say are open to abuse.
It is not the sums involved but the backroom fundraisers and accountants who are now coming in for scrutiny.
They are accused of closing their eyes to shady practices and dodgy foreigners in the interests of filling party coffers.
Labour, buoyed by the success of its attacks on Prime Minister John Major's party over sleaze, want a review of party funding by a parliamentary standards watchdog.
Major rejects calls for a review and says Labour is hypocritical in its allegations.

The Conservatives say that union funding for Labour, and sponsorship of individual members of parliament -- a practice which began before MPs received a salary -- give unions a disproportionate influence on Labour policy.
Major levels the same charge at Blair, who set up a blind trust to channel donations from wealthy supporters to cover his office costs as leader of the Labour party.
Blair says the blind trust, designed he argues precisely to avoid charges that donors can exert influence, has been cleared by the parliamentary standards watchdog.
ANTICIPATED EXPENDITURE

The Conservatives and Labour are each expected to spend between 10 and 20 million pounds, dwarfing the estimated three million budget of the Liberal Democrats. But compared to many other countries, the sums are modest.

In the U.S. primary campaign, in which parties select their candidate, President Bill Clinton and his rival, Bob Dole, each spent around $46 million. For the election, which comes after the primaries, they each had $62 million from public funds.
Britain has so far avoided the move in many other countries in western Europe to increase public funding of political parties to create a level playing field.
Instead, it relies on limits on spending by individual candidates and a ban on paid television advertising.
Britain's election spending limits on candidates are among the strictest in the world -- around 8,000 pounds each.
PARTY FUNDING
But national campaign spending by parties is unlimited and there are few restrictions on where they can get their money. It is this that reformers say leaves the system open to corruption.
The annual accounts of the Conservative party show it raised 18 million pounds in donations in 1995/96.

But the party does not detail individual donors. This rule is religiously observed. Even members of the party's board of finance are not told. This secrecy has been strongly defended and widely attacked by the opposition.

When the House of Commons home affairs committee reviewed the rules on party funding three years ago, its Conservative members -- a majority of the committee -- rejected calls for the names of large donors to be detailed.

They concluded: "Total transparency is for practicable reasons unobtainable and in principle even undesirable". However, a former Conservative party treasurer, Lord McAlpine, has lifted a corner of the veil of secrecy in his memoirs.
Allegations that Major asked McAlpine, who has quit the party in protest at Major's European policies, to solicit funds from a Greek shipping tycoon added to the impression of sleaze.
Major has dismissed the charges, saying that as prime minister he has nothing to do with fundraising.

Labour MP David Winnick, launching a recent bill to reform party funding, told parliament: "I want to see change and reform to undermine the sleaze, and the furtive, underhand way in which the Conservative party collects its money."
The Conservatives have been hurt by past disclosures that businessman Asil Nadir gave them 400,000 pounds ($627,000) in the 1980s after he was courted for cash.
Nadir, the former chief of the collapsed Polly Peck conglomerate, is now a fugitive from British justice in the Turkish-controlled northern half of Cyprus.
Labour has sought to contrast the Conservatives' attitude with its practice of naming all donors who give over 5,000 pounds and refusing donations from foreigners.
BOOM IN LABOUR FINANCES

Ironically, Labour's attack on the Conservatives coincides with a boom in the opposition's finances. On top of support from unions, Labour is enjoying a cash bonanza due to a recruitment drive which is bringing in an estimated 2,000 members a week.
In contrast, major corporate donors, anxious to avoid backing the wrong horse in the election race and under pressure from shareholders, have cut contributions to the Conservatives.

Traditional corporate donors like Lucas Industries, car distributor Inchcape, drinks firms Allied Domecq and Whitbread, British Airways Plc and even United Biscuits, for many years the party's biggest supporter, have stopped donations.
Of course, money is not everything. billionaire Sir James Goldsmith's newly formed Referendum Party is reported to have spent at least 20 million pounds on its campaign.
But polls give the party -- which wants a referendum over Britain's links with Europe -- just two percent of the vote and little chance of winning even one parliamentary seat. ($1=6228 Pound)
